overview: Hylaeosaurus (meaning 'woodland lizard') was a herbivorous ankylosaur from the Early Cretaceous of England, living approximately 139–110 million years ago. Known from specimens from the Wealden Group of Sussex, it reached an estimated 5 metres in length and was armoured with osteoderms and spines. It was described by Gideon Mantell in 1833 and holds a remarkable distinction in the history of science: a Hylaeosaurus specimen was one of the three fossils used by Richard Owen in 1841 to define the new grouping Dinosauria.

Hylaeosaurus is placed within Nodosauridae by the PBDB, making it an ankylosaur without a tail club — in contrast to ankylosaurids. Additional possible occurrences have been noted from Germany and France based on Wealden-equivalent strata. The material from the holotype is largely still embedded in rock at the Natural History Museum in London, meaning much of its anatomy remains unknown. Its historical importance is outsized relative to the completeness of the material.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Hylaeosaurus armatus was named by Gideon Mantell in 1833 from a partial skeleton embedded in a block of limestone from the Tilgate Stone of Sussex. The name means 'woodland lizard', reflecting the forested character of the local Wealden environment. The holotype block, still largely unprepared, resides at the Natural History Museum, London.

articles.title: Founding of Dinosauria
articles.body: In 1841, Richard Owen used Hylaeosaurus, together with Megalosaurus and Iguanodon, as the three founding genera for his newly coined group Dinosauria. This makes Hylaeosaurus one of the three original dinosaurs — a cornerstone of palaeontological history. Owen recognised shared features in these taxa that distinguished them from living and other extinct reptiles.

articles.title: Anatomy and Armour
articles.body: The visible armour of Hylaeosaurus includes prominent spines and osteoderms along the neck and back. Its nodosaurid placement suggests the absence of an ankylosaurid tail club. The embedded nature of the holotype means that much of its skeleton remains hidden within rock, limiting anatomical knowledge. Estimated at up to 5 metres long, it was a moderate-sized ankylosaur.

articles.title: Scientific Significance
articles.body: Beyond its role founding Dinosauria, Hylaeosaurus represents an important early ankylosaur from Europe. PBDB data indicates occurrences across the Wealden of England and possible equivalents in Germany and France, suggesting ankylosaurs were widespread across the Early Cretaceous European archipelago. Its full anatomy may eventually be revealed through modern CT scanning of the host block.

record.description: Hylaeosaurus armatus was a quadrupedal armoured herbivore from the Grinstead Clay Formation of southern England. Its name is based on one incomplete, partly articulated skeleton with vertebrae, girdle and limb elements and large spines; most other British Wealden ankylosaur material cannot be referred to it merely by geography.
facts: The holotype lacks a complete skull and much of the limbs.
Large spines were preserved near the shoulder/neck region, but the full armour arrangement is unknown.
Modern revision retains Hylaeosaurus as distinct from Polacanthus.

review.ageReviewNote: The type horizon is Valanginian Grinstead Clay, not a 150-135 Ma interval extending into the Jurassic.
